title: Do Stock Prices Influence Corporate Decisions? Evidence from the Technology Bubble
research_question: Does the non-fundamental component of equity market valuation influence corporate decisions—specifically capital investment, equity issuance, and cash savings? In particular, when stock prices rise above levels justified by fundamentals, do financially constrained firms respond differently from unconstrained firms in their investment, financing, and liquidity policies?
data_description: The analysis uses an unbalanced firm-year panel constructed from Compustat's annual industrial files (P/S/T, Full Coverage, Research) covering 1971–2003, with primary focus on the 1992–2003 window surrounding the late-1990s technology price run-up. The sample is restricted to manufacturing firms in 113 three-digit SIC industries identified as outside the technology paradigm, yielding 1,943 firms and 14,055 firm-year observations. Key variables include capital expenditures scaled by lagged fixed capital, market-to-book (Q), cash flow, net equity and debt issuance, cash holdings and savings, leverage, and a fundamentals-based projection of Q (FundQ) built from lagged firm- and industry-level profitability, sales growth, investment, liquidity, leverage, market capitalization, and industry R&D. Acquisition data come from SDC; analyst earnings forecasts from IBES; aggregate employment and producer prices from the Bureau of Labor Statistics; and input-output relationships from the BEA 1997 Benchmark accounts. Firms are sorted into financially constrained vs. unconstrained groups using payout policy, asset size, bond ratings, and commercial paper ratings.
institutional_context: The setting is the late-1990s technology stock price run-up in U.S. equity markets, during which Nasdaq and broader indexes rose sharply before reversing in 2000. While valuations of telecommunications, software, and computing firms surged amid widespread enthusiasm about new technologies, the price increase spilled over to many traditional manufacturing sectors—'old economy' industries such as energy, chemicals, paper, steel, mining, and tobacco—whose production processes and productivity were not directly transformed by the technological innovations of that period. Contemporaneous research on factor productivity documented no significant fundamental shifts in these non-tech manufacturing industries during the late 1990s, and indicators such as employment, producer prices, sales, and profitability remained near historical trends, even as their price-earnings ratios and market-to-book values rose well above trend before reverting in 2000. Limits to arbitrage, hedge fund behavior, and the entry of less-experienced retail investors have been proposed as channels for this cross-sector valuation contagion.
